topics.title: Introduction and Scope of AS 26
explain: AS 26 prescribes accounting treatment for intangible assets not covered by other standards.
An enterprise must recognise an intangible asset only when specific criteria are met.

Excluded from AS 26: Inventories (AS 2/7), Deferred tax assets (AS 22), Leases (AS 19), Goodwill on amalgamation or consolidation (AS 14/21), Financial assets, Mineral rights, Insurance policyholder contracts, and Termination benefits.
AS 26 applies to software, start-up costs, R&D activities, licensing agreements (motion pictures, patents, copyrights), and underlying intangibles in finance leases after initial recognition.

flow.title: AS 26 Scope Test
steps: Check if asset is intangible
Verify if covered by another standard
If covered elsewhere, exclude from AS 26
If not excluded, apply AS 26 rules

topics.example: A software company purchasing a copyright for a film applies AS 26, but inventory software held for sale is accounted under AS 2.
remember: Goodwill from amalgamation is governed by AS 14, not AS 26.
R&D and motion picture licensing rights fall within AS 26.
mistakes: Classifying software held for resale in the ordinary course of business under AS 26 instead of AS 2.

quiz.q: Which of the following is covered under the scope of AS 26?
o: Intangible assets held for sale in ordinary course of business
quiz.why: R&D activities are explicitly covered under AS 26, whereas the others are governed by AS 22, AS 2, and AS 21 respectively.

quiz.q: Goodwill arising on amalgamation is accounted under which standard?
quiz.why: Goodwill arising on amalgamation is specifically excluded from AS 26 and covered under AS 14 (Revised).

topics.title: Key Definitions in AS 26
explain: Asset: A resource controlled by an enterprise from past events expecting future economic benefit flows.
Monetary Assets: Money held and assets to be received in fixed or determinable amounts of money.
Amortisation: Systematic allocation of the depreciable amount of an intangible asset over its useful life.
Depreciable Amount: Cost of an asset less its residual value.
Useful Life: Either the period time an asset is expected to be used or the number of production units expected from it.
Active Market: A market with homogeneous items, willing buyers/sellers at any time, and publicly available prices.

flow.title: Determining Useful Life
steps: Identify expected usage period
Estimate expected production units
Choose applicable measure of useful life

topics.example: A patent expected to generate cash flows for 5 years or produce 100,000 units has a useful life based on time (5 years) or output (100,000 units).
remember: Depreciable amount = Cost minus Residual Value.
Active market requires homogeneous items, available prices, and willing buyers/sellers.
mistakes: Confusing monetary assets (fixed money return) with non-monetary assets like patents or software.

quiz.q: What is the depreciable amount of an asset?
quiz.why: Depreciable amount is defined specifically as the cost of an asset less its residual value.

quiz.q: Which condition is NOT required for an active market under AS 26?
o: Prices are available to the public
Willing buyers and sellers are normally found at any time
quiz.why: Active market conditions require homogeneous items, willing parties, and public prices, not government price regulation.

topics.title: Definition, Identifiability, Control & Future Economic Benefits
explain: Intangible Asset Definition: An identifiable non-monetary asset without physical substance held for use in production, rental, or admin purposes.
Identifiability: The asset must be clearly distinguishable from goodwill, meaning it is separable or arises from contractual/legal rights.
Control: The enterprise has power to obtain future economic benefits and restrict access of others to those benefits (usually via legal rights).
Staff training and customer loyalty generally fail the control test because employees can resign and customers can switch suppliers.
Future Economic Benefits: May include revenue from sales, cost savings, or other benefits resulting from asset use.

flow.title: Intangible Asset Identification Test
steps: Check non-monetary nature without physical substance
Test for identifiability (separable or legal right)
Assess control to restrict others
Verify probable future economic benefits

topics.example: Costs incurred by Moon Ltd to train staff on GST/Ind AS cannot be capitalised as an intangible asset because staff can resign, so the company lacks control.
remember: Separability or legal/contractual right is needed for identifiability.
Staff training costs are always expensed because control is absent.
mistakes: Capitalising staff training costs believing they create long-term future economic benefits.

quiz.q: Why is staff training cost expensed immediately rather than capitalised as an intangible asset?
o: The cost cannot be measured reliably
The enterprise lacks control over staff who can resign
quiz.why: An enterprise cannot restrict staff from resigning, so it lacks control over the future economic benefits generated by trained employees.

quiz.q: An asset is identifiable if it is:
o: Separable from goodwill or arises from legal rights
Held for sale in ordinary course of business
quiz.why: Identifiability requires the asset to be clearly distinguished from goodwill via separability or legal/contractual rights.

topics.title: Recognition Criteria and Separate Acquisition
explain: Recognition Criteria: Recognise an intangible asset if and only if (1) it is probable that future economic benefits will flow, and (2) cost can be measured reliably.
Initial Measurement: An intangible asset should be measured initially at cost.
Cost of Separately Acquired Asset: Purchase price + import duties/taxes (non-refundable) + directly attributable expenditure (e.g. legal fees).
Deductions: Trade discounts and rebates are deducted to determine total cost.
Exchange for Securities: Recorded at fair value of asset or fair value of securities issued, whichever is more clearly evident.

flow.title: Cost Calculation for Separate Acquisition
steps: Start with gross purchase price
Deduct trade discounts and rebates
Add non-refundable taxes and duties
Add directly attributable legal/prep costs

topics.example: Buying a patent for ₹10 lakhs with ₹1 lakh legal fees and ₹50,000 trade discount results in an initial asset cost of ₹10.5 lakhs.
remember: Trade discounts and refundable taxes are never included in cost.
Initial measurement of intangible assets is always at cost.
mistakes: Including refundable taxes or operating overheads in the initial cost of a separately acquired asset.

quiz.q: Which item is deducted when calculating the initial cost of an intangible asset?
quiz.why: Trade discounts and rebates are deducted from purchase price to arrive at the asset cost.

quiz.q: An intangible asset is initially measured at:
quiz.why: AS 26 mandates that an intangible asset must be measured initially at cost.

topics.title: Acquisition via Amalgamation, Government Grant & Exchange
explain: Amalgamation: Transferee recognises intangible asset meeting recognition criteria even if unrecognised by transferor. If fair value cannot be measured reliably, it is included in goodwill.
Fair Value Determination: Priority is quoted market price > current bid price > recent transaction price > estimated arm's length amount.
Government Grant: Intangible asset acquired free/nominal consideration is recognised at nominal value or acquisition cost plus directly attributable costs.
Exchange of Assets: Measured at fair value unless transaction lacks commercial substance or fair value is not reliably measurable (then carrying amount of asset given up is used).

flow.title: Fair Value Hierarchy for Amalgamation
steps: Check active market for quoted price
Use current bid price if available
Use price of recent similar transaction
Estimate arm's length amount if no market

topics.example: If an airport landing right is granted by government free of charge, it is recorded at nominal value plus any direct legal registration fees.
remember: Unreliable fair value in amalgamation merges into goodwill.
Exchange lacking commercial substance uses carrying amount of asset given up.
mistakes: Recognising an asset in an exchange transaction at fair value when the transaction lacks commercial substance.

quiz.q: If the fair value of an intangible asset acquired in an amalgamation cannot be measured reliably, it is:
quiz.why: AS 26 states that if fair value cannot be measured reliably in purchase amalgamation, the asset is included in goodwill.

quiz.q: An intangible asset acquired free of charge by way of a government grant is recognised at:
o: Nominal value or acquisition cost plus direct expenses
quiz.why: As per AS 12 and AS 26, government grant assets at concessional rates or free are recognized at nominal value or acquisition cost.

topics.title: Internally Generated Intangible Assets & R&D Phases
explain: Internally Generated Goodwill: NEVER recognised as an asset because it is not an identifiable resource controlled at reliable cost.
Research Phase: Original/planned investigation to gain new scientific/technical knowledge. ALL costs are expensed in P&L immediately when incurred.
Development Phase: Application of research findings to a plan/design prior to commercial production.

Capitalisation Criteria: Capitalise development cost ONLY IF enterprise demonstrates technical feasibility, intention, ability to use/sell, future economic benefits, available resources, and reliable cost measurement.
If an enterprise cannot distinguish Research phase from Development phase, treat the ENTIRE expenditure as Research phase (expense it).
Internally generated brands, mastheads, publishing titles, and customer lists are NEVER recognised as intangible assets.

flow.title: Internal Project Evaluation Flow
steps: Incur project expenditure
Is it Research phase? Expense to P&L
Is it Development phase? Check 6 criteria
If all 6 met: Capitalise; else: Expense

topics.example: AB Ltd spent ₹20 lakhs on research for product X. Because it is research phase, the full ₹20 lakhs is expensed in P&L.
remember: Research costs = ALWAYS expense.
Development costs = Capitalise ONLY if ALL 6 criteria are met.
Brands/mastheads/customer lists generated internally = NEVER capitalise.
mistakes: Capitalising research expenses under the assumption that a successful product will emerge later.

quiz.q: If an enterprise cannot distinguish between the research phase and development phase of an internal project, it should:
o: Treat entire expenditure as research phase and expense it
Allocate expenditure 50:50 between P&L and asset
quiz.why: AS 26 mandates that if research and development phases cannot be distinguished, all expenditure is treated as research phase.

quiz.q: Which of the following internally generated items can be recognised as an intangible asset?
o: Development costs meeting all six recognition criteria
quiz.why: Development costs meeting all 6 recognition criteria are capitalised; internally generated goodwill, brands, and customer lists are never recognised.

topics.title: Cost of Internally Generated Asset & Expense Recognition
explain: Cost includes expenditure incurred from the date the asset first meets recognition criteria.
Reinstatement Prohibited: Expenditure previously recognised as an expense cannot be reinstated later as part of asset cost.
Eligible Costs: Materials, labour/salaries directly engaged, legal registration fees, and directly allocable overheads.
Ineligible Costs (Expense to P&L): Selling/admin overheads, identified inefficiencies/initial operating losses, and staff training costs.
Expenses to P&L on creation: Start-up costs, preliminary legal costs, pre-opening/pre-operating costs, advertising/promotional costs, and relocation expenses.

flow.title: Determining Capitalisable Internal Costs
steps: Identify date recognition criteria met
Accumulate direct materials, labour, overheads
Exclude selling, admin, training, inefficiencies
Capitalise net qualifying expenditure

topics.example: An enterprise spends ₹9 lakhs before Dec 1 (criteria not met) and ₹1 lakh after Dec 1 (criteria met). Only ₹1 lakh is capitalised; ₹9 lakhs is expensed and can never be reinstated.
remember: Prior expensed amounts can NEVER be reinstated into asset cost.
Advertising, start-up, and training costs are expensed immediately.
mistakes: Attempting to capitalise advertising or training expenses incurred to launch a new product.

quiz.q: Expenditure incurred on an internal project prior to meeting recognition criteria:
o: Can be reinstated into asset cost once criteria are met
Must be expensed and can never form part of asset cost
Is deferred in balance sheet as asset under development
quiz.why: AS 26 strictly prohibits reinstating past expenditure that was initially expensed.

quiz.q: Which of the following costs forms part of the cost of an internally generated intangible asset?
o: Salaries of personnel directly engaged in generating the asset
Initial operating losses before planned performance
quiz.why: Direct labour salaries engaged in generating the asset are capitalisable, while selling/admin, training, and operating losses are expensed.

topics.title: Subsequent Expenditure & Subsequent Measurement
explain: Subsequent Measurement Model: Carried at cost less accumulated amortisation and accumulated impairment losses.
Subsequent Expenditure Rule: Expensed when incurred.
Exception to Rule: Add to carrying amount ONLY IF it is probable expenditure will enable asset to generate future economic benefits beyond originally assessed standard AND can be measured reliably.
Subsequent expenditure on brands, mastheads, customer lists is ALWAYS expensed to avoid recognising internal goodwill.

flow.title: Subsequent Expenditure Test
steps: Incur expenditure post-purchase/completion
Check if benefits exceed original performance standard
Check if expenditure is reliably measurable
If both YES: Capitalise; else: Expense to P&L

topics.example: Upgrading a software program to add major missing capabilities that increase efficiency beyond initial assessment is capitalised; routine bug fixes are expensed.
remember: Subsequent expenditure is capitalised only in rare cases.
Carrying amount = Cost - Accumulated Amortisation - Accumulated Impairment.
mistakes: Capitalising routine maintenance or small upgrades on existing software instead of expensing them.

quiz.q: Subsequent expenditure on an intangible asset after purchase is generally:
o: Expensed when incurred unless specific enhancement criteria are met
quiz.why: AS 26 states subsequent expenditure is expensed unless it enhances performance beyond original assessment and is reliably measurable.

quiz.q: After initial recognition, an intangible asset is carried at:
o: Cost less accumulated amortisation and accumulated impairment losses
Fair value at each balance sheet date
quiz.why: AS 26 specifies carrying amount as cost minus accumulated amortisation and accumulated impairment losses.

topics.title: Amortisation Period, Method, Residual Value & Review
explain: Amortisation Period: Depreciable amount allocated over useful life starting when available for use.
10-Year Presumption: Rebuttable presumption that useful life will not exceed 10 years. If rebutted, amortise over useful life, test annually for impairment, and disclose reasons.
Legal Rights Limit: Useful life cannot exceed legal right period unless renewable and renewal is virtually certain.
Amortisation Method: Reflects pattern of benefit consumption (SLM, WDV, Unit of production). Default is Straight-Line Method if pattern is not reliable.
Residual Value: Assumed to be ZERO unless 3rd party commitment exists OR active market exists with probable end-of-life existence.
Review: Review amortisation period and method at least at each financial year-end. Changes are accounted under AS 5.

flow.title: Amortisation Setup Flow
steps: Determine useful life (max 10 years presumption)
Determine residual value (default zero)
Select amortisation method based on benefit pattern
Calculate periodic amortisation charge
Review period & method at year-end

topics.example: An exclusive 60-year hydroelectric right is amortised over 60 years because clear long-term demand rebuts the 10-year presumption.
remember: Default presumption useful life <= 10 years.
Default residual value = ZERO.
Default method = Straight-Line Method.
mistakes: Assuming a non-zero residual value without a third-party commitment or an active market reference.

quiz.q: Under AS 26, the rebuttable presumption is that the useful life of an intangible asset will not exceed:
quiz.why: AS 26 adopts a rebuttable presumption that useful life does not exceed ten years from when available for use.

quiz.q: The residual value of an intangible asset is assumed to be zero UNLESS:
o: There is a third-party purchase commitment or active market
quiz.why: Residual value is assumed zero unless a third party committed to purchase it or an active market exists to determine it.

topics.title: Impairment, Retirements, Disposals & Disclosures
explain: Impairment Testing (AS 28): Calculate impairment loss when carrying amount exceeds recoverable amount.
Mandatory Annual Impairment Test: Required at year-end for (1) intangible assets not yet available for use, and (2) assets amortised over >10 years.
Derecognition: Derecognise asset from balance sheet on disposal or when no future benefits are expected from use/disposal.
Gain/Loss on Disposal: Net disposal proceeds minus carrying amount, recognised in P&L.
Disclosures Required: Amortisation rates/useful lives, amortisation methods, gross carrying amount & accumulated amortisation, opening/closing reconciliation, and R&D expense total.

flow.title: Derecognition & Disposal Accounting
steps: Asset disposed or no future benefit expected
Calculate carrying amount at date of disposal
Deduct carrying amount from net disposal proceeds
Recognise gain/loss directly in P&L

topics.example: Software under development costing ₹10 Cr has recoverable amount drop to ₹6 Cr. An impairment loss of ₹4 Cr (or excess carrying amount over ₹6 Cr) is recognised in P&L.
remember: Assets not yet available for use MUST be tested for impairment annually.
Gain or loss on retirement = Net Proceeds minus Carrying Amount.
mistakes: Skipping annual impairment tests for assets under development claiming they are not yet complete.

quiz.q: Which intangible asset MUST be tested for impairment at least annually even if there is no indication of impairment?
o: An intangible asset not yet available for use
quiz.why: AS 26 mandates annual impairment testing for assets not yet available for use and assets amortised over >10 years.

quiz.q: Gain or loss arising from disposal of an intangible asset is calculated as:
o: Net disposal proceeds less initial cost
Net disposal proceeds less carrying amount
Gross carrying amount less residual value
quiz.why: Gain or loss is the difference between net disposal proceeds and carrying amount of the asset at disposal.
